points: Television: free-to-air channels, which anyone with a television can watch, and subscription or pay-per-view services that charge for access.

Internet and streaming: live streams, highlights and on-demand video.

Podcasts: long-form discussion and interviews about sport.
Elite coverage: live broadcasts, highlights, expert analysis and celebrity athletes.
Elite coverage concentrates on a few popular men's sports, which drives sponsorship and funding for those sports.
Mass-participation coverage is limited and mostly local or charity-focused.

Positive: visible athletes act as role models and inspire people to try a sport.
Positive: coverage raises awareness of activities and events that people can join.
Negative: unequal coverage can make some activities and groups invisible, so people conclude those sports are not for them.

notes.b: The media help decide which sports are seen as suitable for men and for women.
points: Gender stereotype: a fixed belief about which sports and behaviours suit men and women.
Example: men are portrayed as strong and aggressive, while women are portrayed as graceful and suited to 'feminine' sports.
Stereotypes shape which sports people consider suitable for themselves.
Women's sport receives much less coverage than men's, so it seems less important.
Commentary focuses on women's appearance, relationships or emotions rather than their performance.
Sexualised images of female athletes are used to attract attention.
Male-as-norm language: 'football' means men's football, while 'women's football' has to be specified.
Men in aesthetic sports are described as unusual rather than as skilled athletes.
Growing live coverage of women's sport on television and online shows women's competitions as worth watching.
Campaigns for visibility press media to cover women's sport and to present female athletes as skilled performers.
Free-to-air television reaches large audiences without a subscription, which promotes the sport to new viewers.
Pay-per-view and subscription services raise money for the sport through fees, which can fund its development.
Pay-per-view limits access, because viewers who cannot afford a subscription cannot watch.
In Ireland, Gaelic games are shown both on free-to-air television and on a subscription streaming service (GAAGO).

notes.h: Characteristics that give media and spectator appeal
points: Fast pace and continuous action keep viewers engaged.
High scoring or dramatic moments create excitement.
Clear, easily understood rules help new viewers follow the game.
Star players and rivalries give viewers people and stories to follow.
National or local identity, such as county or country, gives viewers a reason to support.
Short duration or a fit for a broadcast slot makes a sport easy to schedule.
Spectacular skills that stand out on camera.
Close contests and unpredictability keep the outcome uncertain.
Suitability for cameras, with a playing area the camera can follow.
Good venues and atmosphere make live attendance appealing.
Four characteristics for hurling: speed, skill, physical contest and county identity.
Shorter formats: Twenty20 is a shortened form of cricket that gives a faster match.
Rule changes that speed up play.
Scheduling for television, so that matches are timed for broadcast slots.

notes.h: Positive impact of coverage on spectator behaviour
points: Inspires attendance and participation, as spectators want to play what they watch.
Builds knowledge and appreciation of skills, so spectators understand what good play looks like.
Creates fan communities that share the sport online and at venues.
Promotes fair play through visible sanctions, when broadcasts show penalties being applied.

notes.h: Negative impact of coverage on spectator behaviour
points: Sensationalises rivalries and controversy, which can raise tension between supporters.
Broadcast replays of contested decisions can inflame a crowd.
Online abuse of players and officials on social media.
Fans may stay at home rather than attend, because they can watch on television.
Copying poor behaviour seen on television, such as dissent towards officials.
Example of a positive overall effect: a live televised match brings new supporters into a club.
Example of a negative overall effect: a heated replay of a decision leads to crowd trouble at the next local fixture.
The overall effect depends on framing: coverage that focuses on skill and fair play encourages positive behaviour, while coverage that focuses on conflict encourages negative behaviour.

questions.prompt: Provide an analysis of how spectator behaviour has been affected by media coverage.
questions.model: Media coverage has affected spectator behaviour in both directions. On the positive side, coverage inspires attendance and participation, because spectators want to play what they watch. It builds knowledge and appreciation of skills, so spectators understand good play and respect it. It creates fan communities that share the sport online and at venues, and it promotes fair play when broadcasts show penalties being applied. On the negative side, coverage sensationalises rivalries and controversy, which raises tension between supporters. Broadcast replays of contested decisions can inflame a crowd, and social media allows abuse of players and officials. Coverage also means fans may stay at home rather than attend, and viewers may copy poor behaviour such as dissent towards officials. The balance depends on framing: coverage that focuses on skill and fair play tends to produce positive behaviour, while coverage that focuses on conflict tends to produce negative behaviour. On balance, the positive effects of coverage are strongest when the focus is on the sport itself.

questions.prompt: Describe, using two examples, the role of the media in maintaining gender stereotypes of women in sport.
questions.model: First example: women's sport receives much less coverage than men's, so it appears less important and women's competitors are less visible as role models. Second example: commentary focuses on women's appearance, relationships or emotions rather than their performance, which reinforces the idea that women are judged by how they look rather than how well they play. Sexualised images of female athletes, and male-as-norm language in which 'football' means men's football, also reinforce the stereotype that women's sport is secondary.

questions.prompt: Identify four characteristics of a named physical activity that give it media or spectator appeal.
questions.model: Activity: hurling. Speed: the game moves quickly, with continuous action that keeps viewers engaged. Skill: spectacular striking and catching stand out on camera. Physical contest: close, physical contests create drama and unpredictability. County identity: supporters follow their county, which gives viewers a reason to watch and attend.
